tracks.title: Center and spread
tracks.summary: This path is for where a set of numbers sits and how wide they are. By the end you can read the mean, the median, and the mode, treat higher moments as averages of spread and skew, and see why a sample variance divides by n − 1.

steps.title: Mean, Median, and Mode
steps.note: We often describe data by their averages: numerical summaries that answer where the numbers sit. The mean, the median, and the mode are three such answers; they line up when the numbers are roughly balanced, and they pull apart when the shape is not. When they disagree, the next question is what other kinds of average can capture spread and shape, not only center.
steps.demoDescription: Move the points and watch which average shifts.
steps.imageAlt: Dot plot of a mildly right-skewed sample. A dotted line marks the mode at 5, a dashed line marks the median at 6, and a solid line marks the mean at 6.94, pulled right by the tail.

steps.title: Moments
steps.note: There are different types of averages, and in statistics those averages of powers of the values (or of their deviations) are called moments. The mean is the first moment; higher moments give numbers for spread and for skew. Raising the deviations to a higher power, or changing the center and the scale, is what turns that average into the variance, the skewness, or the kurtosis. Those numbers still treat the sample mean as if it were already known, which matters once variance is estimated from the same data.
steps.demoDescription: Change the sample and compare how each moment responds.
steps.imageAlt: Three panels of one sample, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 9. The first marks the mean at 4. The second shows squared deviations from that mean, which average to 6.67. The third shows cubed deviations, where the value 9 produces a cube of 125 and the average is 15.

steps.title: Bessel's Correction
steps.note: When we use the data to estimate how spread out they are, the usual average of squared deviations is a little too small, because the sample mean was taken from those same values. Dividing by n − 1 instead of n corrects for that.
steps.demoDescription: Run many samples and see which divisor lands nearer the true variance on average.
steps.imageAlt: Two bars for the average variance estimate from 8000 samples of size 10, drawn from a population whose variance is 100. Dividing by n averages about 90.2, below the true-variance line. Dividing by n − 1 averages about 100.2, on that line.

tracks.title: Shape and pictures
tracks.summary: This path is for the shape of a set of numbers, in a number and in a picture. By the end you can see skew pull the averages apart, read a histogram beside a boxplot, mark an outlier with a fence, and follow the same pile as a smooth density.

steps.title: Skewed Distribution
steps.connectionTitle: When a long tail pulls the mean
steps.note: Not every set of numbers is balanced around its center; a long tail on one side pulls the mean toward itself, so mean, median, and mode sit in different places. That imbalance is skew. A number for skew is useful, but the same shape is easier to see in a picture of how the values pile up and where the middle of the data sits.
steps.demoDescription: Drag the skew and watch the three averages separate.
steps.imageAlt: A right-skewed density curve. A dotted line marks the mode at 0.49, a dashed line marks the median at 1.00, and a solid line marks the mean at 1.44, farther into the long tail.

steps.title: Boxplot and Histogram
steps.note: Numbers for center, spread, and skew summarize a shape; pictures show that shape directly. A histogram shows how values pile up; a boxplot packs the center and spread of the same data into a box and whiskers. Reading both together also shows how far a point can sit before it looks unusual against the middle of the data.
steps.demoDescription: Read the pile and the box together on one sample.
steps.imageAlt: Histogram and boxplot of the same 44 values. The tallest bar is at 5. Dashed lines mark the first quartile at 5, the median at 6, and the third quartile at 8. Whiskers run from 3 to 12.

steps.title: Boxplot and Outliers
steps.note: Once you can see the middle of the data in a boxplot, the next question is which points sit so far out that they count as unusual. The whiskers mark how far a point can sit from the quartiles before it counts as an outlier; the fence is a multiple of the spread inside the box. The histogram’s bars still depend on where the bin edges fall. A smooth curve can follow the same pile without those cuts.
steps.demoDescription: Add extreme points and watch which ones fall outside the fences.
steps.imageAlt: Vertical boxplot for one sample. The box runs from the first quartile at 20 to the third quartile at 40, with the median at 30. Dashed Tukey fences sit at −10 and 70. The upper whisker stops at 44, inside the fence, and a point at 80 is marked as an outlier.

steps.title: Kernel Density Estimate (KDE)
steps.connectionTitle: A smooth curve, not bin edges
steps.note: A histogram’s bars move when the bin edges move, even though the numbers have not. A kernel density estimate sets a small kernel on each point and adds those kernels, so the same pile becomes a smooth curve. The bandwidth h is how wide each kernel is: a narrow kernel keeps the spikes, and a wide one flattens them. The kernel’s shape — Gaussian, Epanechnikov, or boxcar — is how the weights fall away from each point. That same curve is the violin, and a half of it is the cloud in a raincloud plot. The box beside them is still the five-number summary, which is what makes an extreme point look unusual.
steps.demoDescription: Change the sample, the bandwidth, and the kernel. The histogram, the smooth curve, the violin, and the raincloud update together.
steps.imageAlt: Histogram and Gaussian kernel density of the same 44 values as the boxplot figure. Bars are one unit wide and the tallest is at 5. The smooth curve peaks near 5.4. The bandwidth is h = 0.95.

tracks.title: Same summaries, different graphs
tracks.summary: This path is for when the numbers match and the picture does not. By the end you can use a Q–Q plot to compare a sample with a reference curve, and see why the same means, spreads, and correlation can still hide a different graph.

steps.title: Q–Q Plot
steps.connectionTitle: The sample against a reference curve
steps.note: A few extreme points are one way a set of numbers can look unusual; another is that the overall shape does not match a familiar reference curve. A Q–Q plot lines the sample’s quantiles up against a reference distribution, often the normal. A curve away from the straight line means the sample’s shape and the reference shape differ. That check still describes one sample. The next question is whether another picture could carry the same means, the same spread, and the same correlation.
steps.demoDescription: Compare the sample quantiles to the reference line.
formulae: plot (theoretical quantile, sample quantile) for each order statistic
steps.imageAlt: Q–Q plot of one sample of 40 standard normal draws. Ordered sample quantiles are plotted against normal theoretical quantiles and lie close to a straight reference line.

steps.title: Limitations of summary statistics
steps.note: A Q–Q plot can show that a sample’s shape and a reference shape differ. Summaries of center, spread, and correlation can still agree while the pictures do not. Anscombe’s quartet (Anscombe, 1973) and the Datasaurus dozen (Matejka & Fitzmaurice, 2017) keep the means, the standard deviations, and r fixed, and the graph changes from a line to a curve, a stack, a star, or a dinosaur. When the averages match, the graph is still part of the description.
steps.demoDescription: Switch shapes and those summaries stay put. Drag a point and they move; re-lock them and the strange picture can return with the same numbers.
formulae: same x̄, sₓ, ȳ, sᵧ, and r across shapes
steps.imageAlt: Four scatter plots of Anscombe’s quartet. Panel I is a noisy line, II a curve, III a line with one high point, and IV a vertical stack with one point far to the right. The same dashed regression line is drawn on each panel. Every panel has mean x 9.00, mean y 7.50, standard deviations 3.32 and 2.03, and correlation 0.82.

tracks.title: From process to distribution
tracks.summary: This path is for how a statistical claim is built, from a process to a curve. By the end you can name the levels from a parameter to inference, see what fixes a normal curve, and place that curve among the distributions it connects to.

steps.title: The 5-Level Conceptual Hierarchy of Statistics
steps.note: A statistical claim is built in levels. A parameter is a fixed rule of the process. The process produces one outcome. A random variable turns that outcome into a number. The distribution is the pattern of those numbers. Inference uses the sample to say something about the parameter you cannot see. The next step builds one such distribution, the normal curve, from a center and a spread.
steps.demoDescription: Step through a random walk or coin tosses. Each level updates from the parameter through to the inference.
steps.imageAlt: Four panels for a 50-step random walk before any trial. Level 0 sets an up-step probability of 0.50, mean 0, and variance 50, and level 2 reads the end position as X = 2K − N. Level 1 is an empty position plot with a dashed line at 0. Level 3 is a normal curve for the end position, with a dashed line at the mean and dotted lines one standard deviation out. Level 4 marks the true mean at 0 and shows sample size 0.

steps.title: Building the Normal Distribution
steps.connectionTitle: A curve fixed by center and spread
steps.note: Many descriptions of data end by asking whether the shape looks like a familiar smooth curve. The normal distribution is one such curve, fixed by a center and a spread. Putting the curve together shows what the model is made of. The next step places that curve among the other distributions it connects to.
steps.demoDescription: The demonstration puts a normal curve together from a center and a spread.
steps.imageAlt: Standard normal density. A dashed line marks the center at μ = 0. Dotted lines mark one standard deviation on either side, at −1 and 1.

steps.title: Probability Distributions Map
steps.connectionTitle: The normal curve among the others
steps.note: The normal curve is one model among many. This map places sixteen common distributions in five neighborhoods and draws three kinds of link: a special case that fixes a parameter, a transformation or a sum, and a limit. Binomial(n, p) with n = 1 is Bernoulli(p). As n grows and np settles on λ, the binomial count approaches Poisson(λ). As n grows, the binomial count also approaches a normal curve, the shape the previous step built.
steps.demoDescription: Filter a neighborhood, or select a distribution and read its links: a special case, a transform, or a limit.
formulae: Binomial(n, p) → Poisson(λ) as n → ∞ and np → λ
Binomial(n, p) → Normal as n → ∞ (de Moivre–Laplace)
steps.imageAlt: Sixteen distributions in five neighborhoods: coin flip, arrivals, boundaries, the natural world, and the toolbelt. Solid arrows are special cases, dashed arrows are limits, and dotted arrows are transforms. Normal is shaded, and the side panel is its density with mean 0 and standard deviation 1.

tracks.title: Counts, arrivals, and the board
tracks.summary: This path is for counts of coin tosses and of arrivals, and the board that piles those counts into a bell. By the end you can read a binomial count, a Poisson count, and the same kind of sum as bins on a Galton board.

steps.title: Binomial Distribution & Bernoulli Process
steps.note: A coin toss is a Bernoulli trial: two outcomes, the same chance of heads every time, and no memory of the tosses before it. Count the heads in n tosses and that count is binomial, the sum of those trials. The bars are the exact probabilities. The next step counts arrivals in a stretch of time instead of successes in a fixed number of trials.
steps.demoDescription: Set the number of coins and the chance of heads, then run many trials. The observed frequencies settle onto the bars.
formulae: P(X = k) = C(n, k) · pᵏ · (1 − p)ⁿ⁻ᵏ
steps.imageAlt: Left: ten coins, five heads then five tails, so this sequence has 5 heads. Right: binomial probabilities for n = 10 and p = 1/2. The bars peak at k = 5. A normal curve sits on them, with a dashed line at μ = 5 and dotted lines at μ ± σ.

steps.title: Poisson Distribution & Poisson Point Process
steps.connectionTitle: Arrivals in a stretch of time
steps.note: A coin toss fixes the number of trials and counts the successes. A Poisson process fixes a stretch of time and counts arrivals that have no memory of one another. The waiting time between arrivals is exponential with the same rate, and the count in an interval of length t is Poisson(λt). Chop that interval into many short bins and each bin is nearly a Bernoulli trial. As the bins get finer, the binomial count approaches the Poisson count. The next step writes a binomial count as left and right bounces on a Galton board.
steps.demoDescription: Set the rate and the window and watch the arrivals. The bars are the Poisson probabilities, and a finer binomial count approaches them.
steps.imageAlt: Rain on a tile at 6 drops per second. One window shows four drops, a counting-process step path that ends at 4, and the four arrival times. Beside them, Poisson probabilities for μ = 6: the bar at k = 6 is hatched, a dashed line marks μ = 6, and a Binomial(20, 0.3) curve lies on the bars.

steps.title: Galton Board
steps.connectionTitle: Bounces that pile into a bell
steps.note: Each bead on a Galton board takes a left or right bounce at every peg, the same Bernoulli trial as a coin toss. The bin it reaches is the count of right bounces, a binomial sum of independent steps. With more rows, those counts pile up into a bell shape, and the binomial distribution approximates a normal distribution.
steps.demoDescription: Start the flow or drop a burst, and change the rows. Each bead’s bin is its count of right bounces, and more rows pile those counts into a bell.
steps.imageAlt: Left: a board of 12 rows of pegs. One bead takes six right bounces, then six left bounces, and ends in bin 6. Ticks mark bins 0, 6, and 12. Right: binomial probabilities for n = 12 and p = 1/2. The bars peak at k = 6. A normal curve sits on them, with a dashed line at μ = 6 and dotted lines at μ ± σ.

tracks.title: Sampling distributions and intervals
tracks.summary: This path is for what repeated samples do to a summary. By the end you can see sample means settle toward a normal curve, a chi-square as a sum of squared standard normals, and a confidence interval as long-run coverage, not a chance for one interval.

steps.title: Central Limit Theorem (CLT)
steps.note: A single sample mean is one summary of one set of numbers. If you imagine drawing many samples of the same size, those means themselves form a distribution. As each sample gets larger, that distribution of means settles toward a normal curve, whatever shape the raw observations had. The central limit theorem is that statement about means. The spread of those means is the standard error, σ / √n, so a larger sample pulls them in tighter.
steps.demoDescription: Draw many samples and watch their means settle toward a normal curve. This simulation uses the population standard deviation; with one real sample that spread is estimated by s / √n.
formulae: X̄ ≈ N(μ, σ²/n) for large n
steps.imageAlt: Sampling distributions of the mean for an exponential population with mean 1. The n = 2 curve is low and right-skewed, n = 8 is taller, and n = 32 is a tall narrow curve on the dashed line at μ = 1.

steps.title: Horowitz (1974) CLT Simulation
steps.note: The central limit theorem is easier to trust when you can watch sample means accumulate. Horowitz's 1974 classroom simulation draws samples of 10 again and again from about 1,000 scores, roughly N(50, 15.8); the collection of sample means takes on a normal shape. The spread of those means is about σ / √10. Each sample also estimates that spread with s / √n, and the average of those estimates settles near it (Horowitz, 1974, pp. 179–182). Once means behave like normals, sums of squared standard normals become the next building block.
steps.demoDescription: Draw samples of 10 with replacement from about 1,000 scores and watch the means pile up. Each sample’s s / √n estimates the spread of those means.
formulae: X̄ₙ → N(μ, σ²/n) as n grows
steps.imageAlt: Histogram of 96 sample means. Each mean is from 10 draws of a normal population with mean 50 and standard deviation 15.8. A normal curve centered at 50 with standard deviation 5 lies over the bars.

steps.title: Chi-Square Distribution
steps.note: Not every sampling story is about a mean. Square independent standard normal draws and add them up; the sum follows a chi-square distribution, the usual sampling model for a variance. With sampling distributions for means and for variances in view, you can ask what kind of interval claim a sampling distribution can support.
steps.demoDescription: Set the degrees of freedom and draw samples. Each draw squares that many standard normals and adds them.
steps.imageAlt: Chi-square densities for 1, 3, and 5 degrees of freedom. The 1-df curve spikes at zero and runs off the top of the axes. The 3-df curve peaks near 1. The 5-df curve peaks near 3 and sits lower and further right.

steps.title: Target Analogy of Confidence Intervals
steps.note: A confidence interval is a range computed from a sample. In the target analogy the unknown value stays fixed and each interval is a shot, so the stated percentage describes the procedure over many samples — not the chance that this one interval covers that value.
steps.demoDescription: Generate many intervals aimed at a fixed value, and count how many of them cross it.
steps.imageAlt: Twenty horizontal intervals of equal width aimed at a dashed line, the true value. Nineteen solid intervals cross that line. The top interval is dotted, lies entirely to the right, and is labeled miss.

tracks.title: t-test
tracks.summary: This path is for comparing two means when the spread is estimated, so the reference curve has heavier tails. By the end you can say whether the scores come from two groups or the same people.

steps.title: z-Distribution vs t-Distribution
steps.note: When a mean is compared against a known standard deviation, a z curve is the usual reference. In practice that standard deviation is almost always estimated from the same data, and the extra uncertainty shows up as heavier tails than z. When that estimate of the spread comes out small, the statistic is pushed farther into the tail. Those tails are heavier still in a small sample; that wider curve is the t distribution, and it is the reference you will use for the two comparisons that follow.
steps.demoDescription: Compare the z curve with the t curve, and see a small estimate of the spread push the statistic farther into the heavier tail.
steps.imageAlt: The standard normal and a t distribution with 4 degrees of freedom. The left panel shows both full curves. The right panel zooms into the right tail, where the dashed t curve stays above the solid z curve.

steps.title: Independent Samples t-Test
steps.connectionTitle: Two groups that do not share people
steps.note: One common comparison is two groups that do not share people — each person is in one group only. An independent-samples t-test asks whether the two group means differ by more than you would expect from the spread within the groups, using a t curve whose standard error combines those two spreads. A different design pairs two scores within the same person instead.
steps.demoDescription: Compare two groups that do not share people, and see whether their means differ by more than the spread within the groups.
steps.imageAlt: Two groups of eight scores. Group 1 is centered at 50 and group 2 at 62, with an arrow marking a mean difference of 12. A bracket of length s = 4.9 sits beside each mean.

steps.title: Paired Sample t-Test
steps.note: In a paired design, the two scores from each person become one difference. That removes person-to-person variation before the mean difference is set against a t curve. The path ends here: the same family of reference curve, and two designs for which scores enter the comparison.
steps.demoDescription: Turn each person’s two scores into one difference, and set the mean of those differences against a t curve.
steps.imageAlt: Left: eight before-and-after pairs joined by lines. Right: those eight differences, with a dashed line at the mean difference of 5. The two differences equal to 7 are drawn side by side.

tracks.title: Statistical power
tracks.summary: This path is for the chance of detecting a real effect, from the definition to how that chance grows. By the end you can say what power is and what a larger effect or sample does to it.

steps.title: Statistical Power
steps.connectionTitle: The chance of detecting a real effect
steps.note: A significance cutoff is set under the null, but a real effect shifts the sampling distribution of the test statistic. Power is the chance of detecting an effect that is really there: the share of that alternative distribution that lands beyond the null cutoff. Once that definition is clear, the next question is how power changes when the study changes.
steps.demoDescription: A real effect shifts the sampling distribution, and the demonstration shades the share that lands beyond the null cutoff.
steps.imageAlt: A null sampling curve centered at 0 and an alternative curve centered at 2, for σ = 5 and n = 30. A dotted line marks the one-tailed 5% cutoff at 1.50. Gray shading under the alternative, to the right of the cutoff, is the power, about 71%.

steps.title: Power Curve
steps.connectionTitle: Power moves with effect and sample
steps.note: Power is not a fixed number; it moves with the study. A larger effect or a larger sample moves the alternative distribution farther past the null cutoff, and more of it counts as a detection.
steps.demoDescription: A power curve shows how the chance of detecting a real effect changes with the size of the effect and the size of the sample.
formulae: power rises with |effect| and with n
steps.imageAlt: Power of a two-sided, equal-group t test against total sample size, for Cohen's d = 0.50 and α = 0.05. Dashed guides mark the operating point where power first reaches 0.80, at total N = 128.

tracks.title: ANOVA
tracks.summary: This path is for comparing means, from separate groups to the same people and a split of variation. By the end you can say where the variation comes from and what the usual reading assumes.

steps.title: From t-Test to ANOVA
steps.connectionTitle: The same question for more means
steps.note: With two groups, a t-test asks whether the means differ by more than the scatter inside the groups. ANOVA asks the same kind of question when there may be more than two means: is the variation among group means large relative to the variation left inside groups? When each person is measured more than once, that inside scatter depends on how their scores move together.
steps.demoDescription: Set a two-group comparison beside one with more means, and see whether the variation among means is large relative to the variation inside groups.
steps.imageAlt: Two panels with the same within-group scatter. The left panel has group means at 40 and 60. The right panel has group means at 30, 50, and 70. A short horizontal line marks each mean.

steps.title: From Paired t-Test to RM-ANOVA
steps.note: The difference-score standard deviation already has the pre–post correlation built into it. A more positive covariance shrinks s_D: when scores move together, people who score high at one timepoint tend to score high at the other, so individual change scores stay small — and that smaller s_D is what feeds Residual. The same positive covariance enlarges SS Subjects, because subject sums of squares track how far each person's average sits from the grand mean. Together, SS Subjects and Residual make up within-conditions: the scatter around each timepoint mean. By partitioning out those individual differences, the paired t and repeated-measures ANOVA cut noise that an independent test would leave intact. An independent test treats all of within-conditions as residual.
steps.demoDescription: Slide the pre–post correlation and see a positive covariance shrink the difference-score spread, enlarge SS Subjects, and feed the residual.
formulae: s_D² = s₁² + s₂² − 2 r s₁ s₂

steps.title: Partitioning Sum of Squares in 1-Way, 2-Way, and 3-Way ANOVA
steps.note: To compare several means, it helps to say where the variation in the data comes from. With one factor the total splits into a part between groups and a part left inside groups. With two or three factors, and with between-subjects, within-subjects, or mixed designs, that total breaks into more bricks: each main effect, each interaction, and an error term that matches the stratum. The next step is the 2×2 between-subjects case, two main effects, their interaction, and one error.
steps.demoDescription: The same bricks can be read as a flat linear model, grouped by error stratum, or introduced condition by condition.
formulae: SS_total = sum of the atomic bricks
between-subjects: one error term tests every effect
within-subjects: each repeated factor has its own error stratum
F = MS_effect / MS_error for the matching stratum
steps.imageAlt: Between-subjects, one factor, three groups of ten. A bar proportional to degrees of freedom splits a small hatched brick, SS_A with df = 2, from a larger open brick for subjects within A with df = 27.

steps.title: Two-Way ANOVA
steps.note: Sometimes each observation belongs to a combination of two factors, not one. Two-way ANOVA labels variation with both factors at once: each factor has its own main effect, and the interaction is the pattern that appears only in the combination. The next step is the mixed case, where one factor separates people and the other measures the same people twice. The usual reading of these F tests still depends on conditions on the residuals.
steps.demoDescription: See each factor’s main effect, and the interaction that appears only when the two factors are combined.
formulae: F_A = MS_A / MS_error, and likewise for B and AB
steps.imageAlt: Two panels of 2×2 cell means. On the left the female line runs from 38 to 48 and the male line from 46 to 56, parallel. On the right the lines cross: female runs from 38 to 56 and male from 56 to 38.

steps.title: 2×2 Mixed ANOVA
steps.connectionTitle: One factor for groups, one for time
steps.note: A 2×2 mixed design has one factor that separates people into groups and one factor that measures the same people twice. The group effect is tested against differences between people. The time effect and the group-by-time interaction are tested against how people vary in their change. The same picture can be read as two simple comparisons: the midpoints, and the pre-to-post changes. The usual reading of these F tests still depends on conditions on the residuals.
steps.demoDescription: The demonstration separates a group effect, tested between people, from a time effect and a group-by-time interaction, tested against how people vary in their change.
steps.imageAlt: Ten subjects from pre to post, group A solid and group B dashed, with each person's average on a separate track. The between-subjects bar is a group brick of 80 against an error of 2916. The within-subjects bar splits time 180, the group-by-time interaction 101.25, and error 51.84.

steps.title: ANOVA Assumptions
steps.note: The usual reading of an F test wants residuals that are roughly normal, groups with similar spread, and observations that are independent of each other. Those are the conditions for the standard interpretation — a check on whether the splits and F ratios can be read in the ordinary way. Breaking one of them moves the Type I error under the null, the power under the alternative, or both.
steps.demoDescription: Step through normality, similar spread, and independence, and see the Type I error, the power, or both move when one breaks.
steps.imageAlt: Left: a Q–Q plot of standardized residuals from three groups, close to a straight reference line. Right: those groups as dot plots, with means near 20, 32, and 42 and similar vertical spread.

tracks.title: Association
tracks.summary: This path is for how variables move together, from shared movement to the straight line that minimizes squared error, then to the plane that splits the same total into model and error, and then to a share of variance. By the end, sum of squares is the same idea as variance, and positive correlation widens a sum and narrows a difference.

steps.title: Covariance and Correlation
steps.connectionTitle: Shared movement on a common scale
steps.note: When two variables are measured together, a natural question is whether they tend to move in the same direction. Covariance records that shared movement in the units of both variables; dividing by the two standard deviations turns the record into a correlation on a scale from negative one to one. The size of that correlation also has a meaning in units of variance.
steps.demoDescription: Drag the points and watch the covariance and the correlation change.
steps.imageAlt: Scatter of 36 points with a positive association. Dashed lines mark the mean of x and the mean of y. A label reads r = 0.81, unit-free.

steps.title: Ordinary Least Squares (OLS)
steps.note: A straight line through paired measurements is a claim about how one variable changes with the other. Ordinary least squares chooses the intercept and the slope that make the squared vertical gaps as small as they can be. That minimum is the error sum of squares. The same line splits the total sum of squares into a part the line accounts for and a part left over. The share the line accounts for is the proportion of variance in the outcome that the straight line explains.
steps.demoDescription: Choose the intercept and slope that make the squared vertical gaps as small as they can be, and see the total sum of squares split into the part the line accounts for and the part left over.
formulae: SSE(b₀, b₁) = Σ (yᵢ − b₀ − b₁ xᵢ)²
β̂₁ = Σ (xᵢ − x̄)(yᵢ − ȳ) / Σ (xᵢ − x̄)²
steps.imageAlt: Scatter of 36 points with a solid least-squares line and dotted vertical residuals. A label reads SSE minimized, SST = SSR + SSE.

steps.title: Multiple Regression
steps.connectionTitle: From a line to a plane
steps.note: Ordinary least squares on one predictor draws a line and splits the total sum of squares into the part that line accounts for and the part left over: SST = SSR + SSE. With two predictors the fitted surface is a plane, and the same split is written SST = SSM + SSE. SSM is the sum of squared distances from the fitted values to the mean of Y, and SSE is the sum of squared vertical gaps the plane does not close. R² is the share SSM takes of SST.
steps.demoDescription: Fit a plane to two predictors and see the total sum of squares split into the part the plane accounts for and the part left as vertical gaps.
steps.imageAlt: Three-dimensional scatter of 18 open circles around a light gray fitted plane. Dotted vertical lines mark the gaps from the points to the plane. Axes are labeled x₁, x₂, and y. A boxed label reads Ŷ = b₀ + b₁X₁ + b₂X₂. The title reads Two predictors fit a plane.

steps.title: Variance Explained
steps.connectionTitle: A correlation turned into a share
steps.note: A correlation says how strongly two variables line up; squaring it turns that strength into a share of variance. That square is the proportion of variance in one variable that a straight-line relationship with the other accounts for. The last step stays with variance and asks what happens when sources do not share anything.
steps.demoDescription: Square a correlation and see that share of variance as the part a straight-line relationship accounts for.
steps.imageAlt: Left: 36 points with a fitted straight line and dotted residuals. Right: a bar of the variance in y, hatched for the shared 66 percent and open for the remaining 34 percent. The panel title reads R² = 0.66.

steps.title: Additivity of Variance & SS
steps.note: Sum of squares is simply another way to measure deviation — the same idea as variance, kept as a total rather than an average. Because squared deviations are always positive, those totals add cleanly. The catch is mild: since they are squares, adding or subtracting two variables still has to carry their correlation, which widens a sum and narrows a difference when the association is positive.
steps.demoDescription: Add or subtract two variables and see a positive correlation widen the sum and narrow the difference.
formulae: Var(X + Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y) + 2 Cov(X, Y)
